description: For basic transitive clauses, Kolokuma Izon commonly orders subject, object, verb; English normally orders subject, verb, object.
source: Isoun & Egbuson (2025), Sentence Patterns in Izon Using the “Kolokuma” Dialect as a Case Study, International Journal of Education and Social Science 7(3), pp. 27–36. https://iigdpublishers.com/storage/9YWJhVs36tiJcZ3CvRaepAptCw1XER-metaU2VudGVuY2UgUGF0dGVybnMgaW4gSXpvbiAyNy0zNi5wZGY%3D-.pdf
implementation_notes: Exact example is retained in parallel_corpus.csv; generic transfer runs only when a single final verb is identified.

description: Temporal adverbials and locative/adverbial material may occur before the final Izon verb; English commonly places the verb before these adjuncts.
source: Isoun & Egbuson (2025), Sentence Patterns in Izon Using the “Kolokuma” Dialect as a Case Study, International Journal of Education and Social Science 7(3), pp. 27–36. https://iigdpublishers.com/storage/9YWJhVs36tiJcZ3CvRaepAptCw1XER-metaU2VudGVuY2UgUGF0dGVybnMgaW4gSXpvbiAyNy0zNi5wZGY%3D-.pdf
implementation_notes: The supplied example uses a documented sentence pair; adjunct identification remains heuristic.

description: Izon noun phrases can place a definite/class marker after the noun, unlike English DET + NOUN order. Marker choice may depend on noun class and context.
source: Isoun & Egbuson (2025), Sentence Patterns in Izon Using the “Kolokuma” Dialect as a Case Study, International Journal of Education and Social Science 7(3), pp. 27–36. https://iigdpublishers.com/storage/9YWJhVs36tiJcZ3CvRaepAptCw1XER-metaU2VudGVuY2UgUGF0dGVybnMgaW4gSXpvbiAyNy0zNi5wZGY%3D-.pdf
implementation_notes: Do not assume every occurrence of bi/ma/mi is a determiner; the implementation checks context.

description: A verbless subject–complement pattern may translate into English with an overt copula.
source: Isoun & Egbuson (2025), Sentence Patterns in Izon Using the “Kolokuma” Dialect as a Case Study, International Journal of Education and Social Science 7(3), pp. 27–36. https://iigdpublishers.com/storage/9YWJhVs36tiJcZ3CvRaepAptCw1XER-metaU2VudGVuY2UgUGF0dGVybnMgaW4gSXpvbiAyNy0zNi5wZGY%3D-.pdf
implementation_notes: Exact pair supplied; generic copula insertion is intentionally limited.

description: Izon marks tense/aspect morphologically and/or with post-verbal material; the mapping is not a one-to-one English tense table and varies across studies/dialects.
source: Kwokwo & Werigbelegha (2017), A Morphological Study of Inflectional Features in English and Izọn, Niger Delta Research Digest 12(2), pp. 108–122. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17319901
implementation_notes: General documentation only. Do not generate tense/aspect solely from an unverified suffix.

description: A recent descriptive study of Kolokuma reports -gha for negative statements and kumo for negative imperatives. Negative perfective/future patterns include additional changes.
source: Okotori & Simon (2025), Morphosyntax of Negation in Kolokuma, International Journal of Studies in Advanced Education 4(8). https://scholarsdigest.org/index.php/ijsae/article/view/1152
implementation_notes: The engine recognizes only a narrow verb-stem + gha case; complex negation remains unsupported.

pattern: No obligatory subject-number agreement on verb
description: Comparative research reports that Izon verbs do not inflect for singular versus plural subject in the English manner.
source: Kwokwo & Werigbelegha (2017), A Morphological Study of Inflectional Features in English and Izọn, Niger Delta Research Digest 12(2), pp. 108–122. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17319901
implementation_notes: English output may need subject-verb agreement; Izon generation should not blindly add English -s logic.

description: Izon determiner/article forms and demonstratives are not safely interchangeable without noun-class/context information.
source: The Influence of Izon on the Syntax and Lexis of the English of Izon-English Bilinguals, University of Lagos Institutional Repository. https://ir.unilag.edu.ng/bitstream/123456789/4305/1/The%20Influence%20of%20Izon%20on%20the%20Syntax%20and%20Lexis%20of%20the%20English%20of%20Izon-%20English%20Bilinguals.pdf
implementation_notes: A default bi used for generic English definite article generation is a practical approximation, not a complete noun-class model.

description: Reorder a simple English subject–verb–object clause so the object/adjuncts precede the main verb in Izon.
source: Isoun & Egbuson (2025), Sentence Patterns in Izon Using the “Kolokuma” Dialect as a Case Study, International Journal of Education and Social Science 7(3), pp. 27–36. https://iigdpublishers.com/storage/9YWJhVs36tiJcZ3CvRaepAptCw1XER-metaU2VudGVuY2UgUGF0dGVybnMgaW4gSXpvbiAyNy0zNi5wZGY%3D-.pdf
implementation_notes: A generic rewrite is attempted only if exactly one lexical verb is recognized.

description: English places determiners before nouns; Kolokuma Izon may place its definite/class marker after the noun.
source: Isoun & Egbuson (2025), Sentence Patterns in Izon Using the “Kolokuma” Dialect as a Case Study, International Journal of Education and Social Science 7(3), pp. 27–36. https://iigdpublishers.com/storage/9YWJhVs36tiJcZ3CvRaepAptCw1XER-metaU2VudGVuY2UgUGF0dGVybnMgaW4gSXpvbiAyNy0zNi5wZGY%3D-.pdf
implementation_notes: The implementation uses bi as a conservative default and omits a/an; noun-class-aware determiner generation is future work.

description: English auxiliaries, -ed, and -ing do not map mechanically to one Izon suffix. Published examples attest some common forms, but verb class and aspect matter.
source: Kwokwo & Werigbelegha (2017), A Morphological Study of Inflectional Features in English and Izọn, Niger Delta Research Digest 12(2), pp. 108–122. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17319901
implementation_notes: The code generates only narrow heuristics (past -mi, progressive -yemi); these must be validated by Kolokuma speakers.

description: English often inserts do/does/did for negation; Kolokuma Izon uses verb-associated negation, with different forms for statements and imperatives.
source: Okotori & Simon (2025), Morphosyntax of Negation in Kolokuma, International Journal of Studies in Advanced Education 4(8). https://scholarsdigest.org/index.php/ijsae/article/view/1152
implementation_notes: Simple negative forms only; do not treat past-perfect or future negation as solved.

description: English indefinite articles usually have no direct one-word equivalent in the cited Izon description. Definiteness and number must still be interpreted in context.
source: The Influence of Izon on the Syntax and Lexis of the English of Izon-English Bilinguals, University of Lagos Institutional Repository. https://ir.unilag.edu.ng/bitstream/123456789/4305/1/The%20Influence%20of%20Izon%20on%20the%20Syntax%20and%20Lexis%20of%20the%20English%20of%20Izon-%20English%20Bilinguals.pdf
implementation_notes: The implementation omits a/an rather than emitting an English-style standalone equivalent.

description: In standard English simple-present declarative clauses, a third-person singular subject normally selects an -s/-es form (he runs; Ebi goes), while I/you/we/they take the base form.
source: Standard English descriptive grammar; English target morphology note
implementation_notes: Implemented as a heuristic only when the Izon predicate is not identified as past or progressive; ambiguous tense/aspect still requires context review.

description: English progressive clauses use a form of be plus a present participle; auxiliaries should not be translated as ordinary lexical verbs.
source: Standard English descriptive grammar; paired with Izon morphology research
implementation_notes: The engine uses a narrow -yemi generation heuristic after finding the lexical verb. Native-speaker confirmation is required.

description: English yes/no questions usually use auxiliary inversion or do-support, and wh-questions have additional ordering constraints.
implementation_notes: Questions are not generalized by the current rule engine. Add verified Kolokuma and English question pairs before implementing a transfer rule.

description: English coordinate and subordinate clauses can contain multiple predicates and conjunctions; clause boundaries must be parsed before changing word order.
implementation_notes: The current sentence transfer declines generic reordering when it cannot isolate one main lexical verb.

description: A Kolokuma-focused study reports kumo with negative imperatives and distinguishes them from negative statements using -gha.
source: Okotori & Simon (2025), Morphosyntax of Negation in Kolokuma, International Journal of Studies in Advanced Education 4(8). https://scholarsdigest.org/index.php/ijsae/article/view/1152
implementation_notes: Documented only; current code must not treat kumo as a general negative suffix or claim imperative translation is solved.

description: Izon tone and vowel diacritics can distinguish lexical items; exact spelling should be retained and accentless lookup treated as an ambiguous fallback.
source: Source dictionary orthography and lexical distinctions
implementation_notes: The tokenizer preserves combining marks; dictionary lookup prefers exact forms and falls back to a tone-insensitive key only if needed.

description: Definite plural marker -mo. The supplied example is akasi (chair) → akasimo (the chairs).
implementation_notes: Productive use is available through morphology.py; noun-class restrictions have not been independently checked.

description: Indefinite plural marker -ama. The supplied example is ekpeti (box) → ekpeti-ama (boxes).
implementation_notes: Preserve the hyphen in the supplied example; general use needs speaker review.

description: Plural marker -otu. The supplied example is ogoni (visitor) → ogoni-otu (visitors).
implementation_notes: The example is preserved in data/izon_morphology.csv.

description: Definite plural forms include oweiamini (the men), ereamini and ereaminimọ (the women).
implementation_notes: Some examples are listed as alternate allomorphs; no universal class-selection rule is inferred.

description: Female/gendered singular form; ere → ereabàu (girl/miss).
implementation_notes: Source terminology and example preserved; semantics may be context-sensitive.

description: Female title/form; erearau (Mrs/madam).
implementation_notes: Not treated as an unrestricted productive suffix on every noun.

description: Source-supplied subject forms: Àri (I), Woni (we), Ári (you), Ọ́mịnị (you plural), Eri (he), arau (she), Ọ̀mịnị (they).
implementation_notes: Context-sensitive pronoun mapping has been updated to prefer these supplied forms.

description: Source-supplied object forms: Ì (me), wó (us), Í (you), ó (you plural), Wò/ù (him), árà/á (her), Ò (them).
implementation_notes: Alternatives are retained in the reference; the translator uses one default form where English is ambiguous.

description: Source-supplied forms: Ìnè (my), Wó (our), Ínè/ínè (your), Wò/ù (his), árà/á (her), oro (their).
implementation_notes: Possessive choice is context-sensitive and needs further examples.

description: Source-supplied forms: Wòi (his), árà (hers), ọ̀rèi (theirs); Ìnei (mine/yours), Woi (ours), ọréi (yours).
implementation_notes: The supplied document repeats Ìnei for mine and yours; this is preserved rather than resolved by inference.

description: Source-supplied forms include ìnèọngọ (myself), áràọngọ (herself), and wòọngọ (himself).
implementation_notes: Only documented forms are listed; full person/number paradigm is not inferred.

description: Comparative adjective marker: zau-dẹịn (smaller), ganị-dẹịn (more expensive), sụ-dẹịn (lazier), Ikịsá-dẹịn (shorter).
implementation_notes: Implemented for the four adjective bases explicitly supplied in morphology.py.

description: Superlative adjective marker: zau-fa (smallest), ganị-fa (most expensive), sụ-fa (laziest), Ikịsá-fa (shortest).
implementation_notes: Implemented for the four adjective bases explicitly supplied in morphology.py.

description: Intensifier meaning very: zau-kami, ganịkami, sụkami, Ikịsákami.
implementation_notes: Hyphenation differs between the examples; generated form follows the source example for each root.

description: Intensifier meaning too: zaubọwẹmi, ganịbọwẹmi, sụbọwẹmi, Ikịsábọwẹmi.
implementation_notes: Generated form follows the supplied examples.

description: Adjective negation examples include zaugha/kumo, ganịgha/kumo, sụagha/kumo, and Ikịságha/kumo (not small/expensive/lazy/short).
implementation_notes: The original table formatting gives alternative forms and is ambiguous; the first form is used as the default.

implementation_notes: Explicit example paradigms are available in morphology.py; no broad productive suffix is assumed for all verbs.

implementation_notes: Explicit example paradigms are available in morphology.py.

description: Present-progressive examples: biịyemi (asking), gẹẹyemi (writing), muyemi (going).
implementation_notes: Explicit example paradigms are available in morphology.py.

description: Present-perfect examples: biịdọụ (asked), gẹẹdọụ (written), mudọụ (gone).

implementation_notes: Labels and glosses vary within the source; included as source-specific paradigm data.

implementation_notes: Explicitly supplied forms are available; generated morphology for other verbs remains a heuristic.

description: Interrogative modifiers may follow the head noun or remain in-situ.
implementation_notes: Phrase rule only; do not infer a universal standalone equivalent for which.

description: Use the documented full interrogative construction.
implementation_notes: Retains source spelling; native-speaker validation recommended.

description: Use the documented recipient interrogative construction.
implementation_notes: Context-sensitive; phrase-level only.

description: Use supplied possessive interrogative example.
implementation_notes: Only exact example encoded; do not generalize to all nouns without review.

description: Use documented singular/plural demonstrative phrase forms.
implementation_notes: Examples and plural forms vary by construction; native-speaker review recommended.

description: Prefer explicit closed-class pronoun overrides over dictionary homonyms.
source: User-supplied pronouns (1).docx, Section VI; existing project pronoun overrides
implementation_notes: Existing mappings are context-biased defaults; case, tone, and dialect variants require validation.

description: Documented standard passive pattern; English be + past participle + by-agent.
expected_output: The money was taken by me
implementation_notes: Pattern recorded; generic realization is not guaranteed for every verb.

description: The source describes prị as an alternative/progressive passive marker with pragmatic constraints.
expected_output: Fish was being killed by them
implementation_notes: Source notes prị may be non-standard with inanimate objects; do not apply indiscriminately.

description: A simple clause contains one independent clause and one main predicate. Identify the subject and main verb before translating; do not treat auxiliaries as lexical verbs.
source: Standard English grammar; proposed transfer rule
implementation_notes: Structural inventory only. Add a verified Kolokuma Izon target pattern before enabling generation.

description: Identify subject, lexical verb, and direct object. Translate each constituent, then apply the verified Izon word order; the project currently documents SOV as a common Izon pattern.
source: Standard English grammar; existing project SOV rule
implementation_notes: Do not assume every clause is SOV; validate verb class and constituent roles.

description: A simple intransitive clause has a subject and a verb but no direct object.
implementation_notes: Requires verified Izon lexical verb and tense/aspect mapping.

description: English be links a subject to a noun, adjective, or other complement. Do not translate am/is/are as unknown content words; select an Izon copular or verbless construction based on evidence.
implementation_notes: Target-language copula behavior and article handling must be confirmed for Kolokuma.

pattern: Simple negative: S + AUX + not + V
description: Detect negation as clause-level meaning; do not translate do/does/did as ordinary lexical verbs. Map the negative construction to the documented Izon verb form.
example_input: The child does not eat fish.
implementation_notes: Izon negation is morphology/construction-sensitive; do not apply -gha blindly to every tense/aspect.

pattern: Simple interrogative: AUX + S + V / WH + clause
description: Identify question type (yes/no or wh-question), question word, subject, and predicate before transfer.
implementation_notes: Needs validated Kolokuma templates and separate handling of person, thing, place, time, reason, and choice questions.

pattern: Compound: independent clause + and + independent clause
description: A compound sentence joins two independent clauses. Parse and translate each clause separately, then insert the verified Izon equivalent of the coordinator.
example_input: The child eats fish, and the mother cooks yam.
implementation_notes: Do not translate the whole sentence by token substitution; preserve clause boundaries and punctuation.

pattern: Compound: independent clause + but + independent clause
description: The coordinator but expresses contrast between two independent clauses.
example_input: The child is tired, but the child works.
implementation_notes: Use a verified Kolokuma coordinator; do not assume English conjunctions map one-to-one.

pattern: Compound: independent clause + or + independent clause
description: The coordinator or expresses alternatives between independent clauses.
example_input: We can go now, or we can wait.
implementation_notes: Coordinator and clause ordering require Kolokuma examples.

pattern: Complex: main clause + because + subordinate clause
description: A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. Identify the reason clause and translate both clauses using a verified causal linker.
example_input: The child stayed home because it rained.
implementation_notes: Need verified Izon equivalent and evidence for subordinate-clause order.

pattern: Complex: if + subordinate clause, main clause
description: Identify the condition clause and main clause; preserve conditional meaning and any tense/aspect distinctions.
example_input: If it rains, we will stay home.
implementation_notes: Conditional morphology and clause order must be validated; do not infer future forms from English will.

description: Identify a temporal dependent clause and its boundary; preserve the temporal relation when transferring clause order.
example_input: When the child arrives, we will eat.
implementation_notes: Each temporal linker needs a verified Kolokuma equivalent and example.

description: Identify a noun modified by a relative clause and keep the relative clause attached to the correct noun.
example_input: The woman who came is my mother.
implementation_notes: Relative pronouns and relative-clause order are not covered by the current interrogative-pronoun rules.

description: Identify the reporting predicate and embedded clause; translate the embedded clause as a clause, not as an independent sequence of words.
example_input: I know that the child is sleeping.
implementation_notes: Requires clause embedding, complementizer evidence, and tense/aspect handling.

pattern: Compound-complex: two independent clauses + at least one dependent clause
description: Parse the sentence into at least two independent clauses and one dependent clause before translation. Translate each clause and reconnect them with verified coordinators/subordinators.
example_input: The child stayed home because it rained, and the mother went to the market.
implementation_notes: Requires a clause tree or structured representation; a flat word-by-word pass is insufficient.

description: Detect clause boundaries from conjunctions, subordinators, relative-clause markers, punctuation, and finite predicates before reordering words.
example_input: The child eats fish, but the mother cooks yam.
implementation_notes: Do not split blindly on every occurrence of and/but/or; account for coordinated phrases inside a single clause.

description: Translate each parsed clause using its own subject, predicate, objects, adjuncts, polarity, question type, and tense/aspect, then apply a verified connector and target clause order.
example_input: The child stayed home because it rained.
implementation_notes: This is an architecture rule, not an executable language rule until a parser and validated Izon patterns are supplied.

description: Preserve sentence-final punctuation and commas that mark clause boundaries, while adapting punctuation only where the target-language convention requires it.
example_input: The child stayed home because it rained.
implementation_notes: Punctuation must not determine grammar alone; conjunctions and clause structure should guide parsing.

pattern: Simple clause: NP + (NP / AdjP / adverbial / postpositional phrase) + predicate; verb commonly clause-final in verbal clauses
description: Izon simple sentences in the supplied examples show more than one clause pattern: subject plus predicate; subject plus object/material plus final verb; verbless or copular-like subject–complement expressions; and imperative clauses. For verbal clauses, retain the documented tendency for the predicate verb to occur late/finally and transfer constituents into the appropriate English order. Do not force every simple sentence into one rigid template.
source: User-supplied ijaw machine translation.docx, simple examples; project Izon grammar reference
implementation_notes: The bilingual pair is available in data/parallel_corpus.csv. Phrase labels are provisional; exact NP/VP boundaries and lexical segmentation require Kolokuma speaker review.

pattern: English simple clause: S + V + (O / C / A); copular: S + BE + C; imperative: (you) + V + O
description: Parse English simple clauses into subject, finite/lexical verb, object, complement, and adjuncts. Treat be as a copula rather than an unknown lexical word; treat imperative subjects as optionally unexpressed. Transfer the semantic roles to the appropriate Izon construction, using the documented Izon predicate placement and noun phrase patterns rather than copying English word order.
source: Standard English clause structure; user-supplied ijaw machine translation.docx; project Izon grammar reference
implementation_notes: General generation is not implied by this inventory entry. The exact bilingual example is stored in data/parallel_corpus.csv; validate copula, aspect, and argument order before broad generation.

pattern: Compound: [independent Izon clause] + [Izon coordinator/linker] + [independent Izon clause]
description: The supplied Kolokuma examples form compound sentences by joining two independent clauses. Connectors visible in the examples include kọ̀, ọ̀bọ̀, gbá, kọ́, ọ̀kpọ̀ and related forms. Their meanings are context-sensitive in the source examples; do not assign a one-to-one English equivalent without checking the clause relation. Translate each clause, identify the relation (addition, contrast, result/reason), then produce natural English coordination.
example_input: Ú béì kìmí béì àsàsà bóẹ̀mị, kọ̀ éré má ú kíléẹ̀mị.
expected_output: That man is coming quickly, but the wife is greeting him.
source: User-supplied ijaw machine translation.docx, compound examples 1–30
implementation_notes: Clause-level structural rule; all 30 bilingual pairs are stored in data/parallel_corpus.csv. Connector semantics and clause segmentation require validation.

pattern: English compound: [independent S + V clause] + coordinating conjunction + [independent S + V clause]
description: Recognize two independent English clauses joined by and, but, so, or another coordinator. Parse each clause independently, then map the semantic relation to an attested Izon linker and preserve the clause order found in verified Kolokuma examples. Do not mechanically substitute and/but/so with a single Izon word.
example_input: That man is coming quickly, but the wife is greeting him.
expected_output: Ú béì kìmí béì àsàsà bóẹ̀mị, kọ̀ éré má ú kíléẹ̀mị.
source: Standard English coordination; user-supplied ijaw machine translation.docx, compound examples 1–30
implementation_notes: All 30 bilingual compound pairs are available in data/parallel_corpus.csv. Generic clause recombination is not yet implemented.

pattern: Compound-complex: [dependent/subordinate Izon clause] + [independent clause] + coordinator + [independent clause] (order varies)
description: The supplied compound-complex examples contain at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. Subordinate or temporal/cause relations are signalled by forms in context, including bárá, bá and ásáìn in the provided examples. Preserve the dependency relation and distinguish it from coordination; do not treat every comma-separated segment as an independent clause.
example_input: Bárá fáí mị lá èmí fịẹ́ị, dádá bóẹ̀mị, gbá ú béí kìmí kíléẹ̀mị.
expected_output: Because the fire is hot, father is coming, and he is greeting that man.
source: User-supplied ijaw machine translation.docx, compound-complex examples 1–30
implementation_notes: All 30 source pairs are stored in data/parallel_corpus.csv. Subordinator meanings and clause boundaries are context-dependent and need native-speaker validation.

pattern: English compound-complex: subordinate clause + independent clause + coordinator + independent clause (or another attested ordering)
description: Identify at least two independent clauses and one dependent clause. Classify subordinate relations such as cause (because) and time (while), then identify the coordinating relation between independent clauses. Translate the clauses separately and reconnect them using attested Izon constructions and ordering from the supplied bilingual examples.
example_input: Because the fire is hot, father is coming, and he is greeting that man.
expected_output: Bárá fáí mị lá èmí fịẹ́ị, dádá bóẹ̀mị, gbá ú béí kìmí kíléẹ̀mị.
source: Standard English clause structure; user-supplied ijaw machine translation.docx, compound-complex examples 1–30
implementation_notes: All 30 bilingual compound-complex pairs are available in data/parallel_corpus.csv. Generic multi-clause parsing and generation remain future implementation work.
